questions.explanation: Keeping repayments at the old level means capital continues to be repaid faster, so the balance falls more quickly and less interest accrues in total. Reducing the repayment leaves more capital outstanding for longer.
questions.reference: Overpayments - reduce term vs reduce repayment

questions.question: During a three-month payment break, no repayments are made but interest continues to accrue on the loan. If the original end date stays the same, what is the usual effect when repayments resume?
options: Repayments return to exactly the previous amount and total interest is unchanged
The balance is higher than before the break, so repayments and total interest increase
The accrued interest is written off by the lender
The interest rate is reduced to compensate for the break
questions.explanation: Unpaid interest is added to the balance, so a larger balance must be repaid over a shorter remaining period, increasing repayments and total interest.

questions.question: A borrower in financial difficulty is offered a term extension to reduce monthly repayments. What is the main disadvantage the adviser should point out?
options: The interest rate must convert to a fixed rate
The lender automatically takes extra security
The loan must be repaid in full before the extension starts
More interest is paid over the life of the loan, and the debt may run further into later life or retirement
questions.explanation: A longer term lowers repayments but keeps the debt outstanding for longer, increasing total interest and possibly extending repayments beyond retirement when income may fall.

questions.question: Which statement about high cost credit providers (formerly known as moneylenders) in Ireland is correct?
options: They are exempt from the Consumer Credit Act 1995
They are member-owned co-operatives sharing a common bond
They are licensed by the Central Bank and typically provide small, short-term loans at rates well above mainstream lenders
They usually take the borrower's home as security
questions.explanation: High cost credit providers must hold a Central Bank licence and are subject to consumer credit legislation. They typically lend small amounts over short periods, often to people with limited access to mainstream credit, at a much higher cost.
questions.reference: High cost credit providers - Consumer Credit Act 1995 as amended

questions.question: A 'retail credit firm' authorised by the Central Bank of Ireland is best described as:
options: a shop that sells goods on credit using its own deposit-taking licence
a non-bank firm that provides credit directly to consumers without taking deposits
a credit intermediary that arranges loans but never lends its own money
a firm that lends only to limited companies
questions.explanation: A retail credit firm provides credit directly to consumers (for example personal loans, hire purchase or PCP finance) but is not a bank or credit union and does not take deposits. A credit intermediary only arranges credit.
questions.reference: Retail credit firms - Central Bank authorisation

questions.question: Shane borrows €6,000 for a car at a flat rate of 5% a year over 3 years, repaid in 36 equal monthly instalments. What is his monthly repayment?
questions.explanation: Interest = €6,000 x 5% x 3 = €900, so the total repayable is €6,900; €6,900 / 36 = €191.67. €166.67 is capital only, €175.00 applies only one year's interest, and €25.00 is the monthly interest alone.

questions.question: Two offers are available for a €10,000 loan over 5 years. Offer A: 60 monthly repayments of €195 and no fees. Offer B: 60 monthly repayments of €190 plus a €400 fee paid at the start. Which offer costs less in total, and by how much?
options: Offer A, by €100
Offer B, by €300
Offer B, by €100
They cost exactly the same
questions.explanation: Offer A: 60 x €195 = €11,700. Offer B: 60 x €190 = €11,400 plus €400 = €11,800. Offer A is cheaper by €100; looking only at the lower monthly repayment (a saving of €300 over the term) ignores B's fee.

questions.question: Who bears the interest rate risk under a variable rate loan?
options: The lender, because it cannot change the rate once agreed
The Central Bank, which compensates borrowers for rate rises
The borrower, because repayments can rise if the lender increases the rate
Nobody, because variable rates are capped at the ECB rate
questions.explanation: Under a variable rate the lender can change the rate, so the borrower is exposed to higher repayments if rates rise (and benefits if they fall).

questions.question: A garden centre needs extra cash every spring to buy stock, which it repays from sales by late summer. Which facility best suits this need?
options: A ten-year term loan drawn in full at the start
An overdraft or revolving working-capital facility with an agreed limit
A residential mortgage top-up on the owner's home
A hire-purchase agreement over the stock
questions.explanation: A seasonal, fluctuating working-capital need suits a flexible facility such as an overdraft, where interest is paid only on the amount drawn and the balance clears from sales. A long-term loan would leave the business paying interest on money it does not need for much of the year.

questions.question: Brendan borrows €50,000 on an interest-only basis for 5 years at 6% a year. Interest is paid each year and the capital is repaid at the end. What is the total amount repayable?
questions.explanation: Annual interest is €50,000 x 6% = €3,000, so 5 years' interest is €15,000. Adding the €50,000 capital gives €65,000 in total. €66,911 assumes interest is compounded rather than paid each year.

questions.question: Which is the strongest reason for a borrower to choose a variable rate rather than a fixed rate?
options: Variable rates guarantee the lowest repayments over the full term
Variable rates cannot be increased by the lender
Variable rates are always included in the Central Bank's tracker protection
Flexibility to overpay or switch without breakage charges, and to benefit if rates fall
questions.explanation: Variable rates generally allow overpayments and redemption without breakage costs, and repayments fall if the rate is cut. The trade-off is uncertainty, as the lender may increase the rate.
questions.reference: Fixed vs variable - choosing a rate type

questions.question: In a lender's pricing, what is the 'margin'?
options: The deposit the borrower must provide
The difference between the rate charged to borrowers and the lender's cost of funds, covering costs, risk and profit
The maximum amount the borrower may overpay each year
The ECB main refinancing rate
questions.explanation: A lender's lending rate is broadly its cost of funds plus a margin. The margin must cover operating costs, expected credit losses and the cost of capital, and provide a profit.
questions.reference: Interest rate drivers - cost of funds plus margin

questions.question: What is 'approval in principle' (AIP) from a mortgage lender?
options: A binding loan offer that cannot be withdrawn
An indication of how much the lender is prepared to lend, subject to conditions such as a satisfactory valuation and final checks
Confirmation that the purchase contracts have been signed
The release of the mortgage funds to the buyer's solicitor
questions.explanation: AIP tells the buyer roughly how much they can borrow so they can bid with confidence, but it is conditional. The formal loan offer follows once a property is identified, valued and the application is fully underwritten.
questions.reference: House purchase process - approval in principle

questions.question: Which sequence best reflects the usual steps in buying a home with a mortgage in Ireland?
options: Loan offer, approval in principle, valuation, drawdown, contracts signed
Contracts signed, approval in principle, valuation, loan offer, drawdown
Approval in principle, sale agreed and valuation, loan offer, contracts signed, drawdown and closing
Valuation, drawdown, approval in principle, loan offer, contracts signed
questions.explanation: A buyer usually gets AIP, agrees a sale, the lender values the property and issues a formal loan offer, contracts are signed, and the funds are drawn down for closing. Signing contracts before a loan offer exposes the buyer to losing the deposit if finance falls through.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the valuation a mortgage lender requires before issuing a loan offer?
options: To confirm that the property is adequate security for the loan
To provide the buyer with a full structural survey
To calculate the buyer's Local Property Tax
To fix the stamp duty payable
questions.explanation: The lender's valuation assesses the property's value as security and is used to calculate the LTV. It is not a structural survey, so buyers are advised to commission their own survey.

questions.question: With an annuity (capital and interest) mortgage, if all repayments are made as scheduled:
options: the full capital remains outstanding at the end of the term
a separate investment policy is needed to clear the loan
the loan is repaid in full by the end of the term
only the interest is repaid
questions.explanation: Each annuity repayment covers interest and some capital, so the loan is fully repaid by the end of the term. Interest-only and endowment mortgages leave capital to be repaid from another source.

questions.question: A historic endowment mortgage is best described as:
options: an annuity mortgage with a life cover rider
an interest-only mortgage where the capital is intended to be repaid from the proceeds of an investment-linked endowment policy, with a risk of shortfall
a mortgage repaid from the tax-free lump sum of a pension
a lifetime mortgage for people aged over 60
questions.explanation: With an endowment mortgage the borrower pays interest only to the lender and premiums into an endowment policy expected to repay the capital at maturity. If investment returns disappoint, there may be a shortfall.

questions.question: Under a pension mortgage, the capital is intended to be repaid from:
options: the tax-free lump sum from the borrower's pension at retirement
the State Pension paid weekly
the sale of the property at retirement
a decreasing term life policy
questions.explanation: A pension mortgage is interest-only during the term, with contributions paid into a pension; the capital is intended to be cleared from the retirement lump sum. This reduces the funds available for retirement income.

questions.question: Sorcha and Tadhg have a tight budget and want to know exactly what their mortgage repayment will be for the next five years. Which rate type best meets this objective?
options: Standard variable rate
An interest-only variable rate
A tracker rate
A five-year fixed rate
questions.explanation: A fixed rate keeps repayments the same during the fixed period regardless of ECB or lender rate changes. Variable and tracker rates can rise.

questions.question: A split-rate mortgage is one where:
options: two lenders share the loan equally
the interest rate changes every month
part of the loan is on a fixed rate and the rest on a variable rate
the borrower pays interest only for the first half of the term
questions.explanation: Splitting the loan gives some payment certainty on the fixed portion and flexibility (for example overpayments without breakage charges) on the variable portion.

questions.question: A borrower redeems a fixed-rate mortgage during the fixed period. In which situation is a breakage cost most likely to be payable?
options: Interest rates have fallen since the rate was fixed
Interest rates have risen since the rate was fixed
The loan is on a tracker rate
The borrower is redeeming on the last day of the fixed period
questions.explanation: A breakage cost compensates the lender for its funding loss. If market rates have fallen, the lender can only re-lend the money at a lower rate than it fixed, so it loses out and charges the borrower.

questions.question: Eoin is buying a home valued at €400,000 with a mortgage of €340,000. What is the loan-to-value (LTV) ratio?
questions.explanation: LTV = loan / value = €340,000 / €400,000 = 85%. 15% is the deposit as a proportion of value, and 117.6% is value divided by loan.

questions.question: Why do many lenders offer lower mortgage rates at lower LTVs?
options: Lower-LTV borrowers always have higher incomes
Lower-LTV loans are exempt from mortgage protection requirements
Lower-LTV loans must be on tracker rates
A lower LTV gives the lender a larger equity cushion, so its risk of loss is lower
questions.explanation: The more equity the borrower has, the more the property can fall in value before the lender faces a loss on default, so lower-LTV lending is less risky and can be priced more cheaply.

questions.question: Hannah, a first-time buyer, is buying a home for €350,000. The maximum LTV available to her is 90%. What is the minimum deposit she needs?
questions.explanation: Maximum loan = 90% x €350,000 = €315,000, so the minimum deposit is €35,000 (10%). €315,000 is the maximum loan, not the deposit.

questions.question: Ciara, a first-time buyer, is buying a second-hand house for €380,000. As of 2026, how much stamp duty is payable?
options: Nil, because first-time buyers are exempt
questions.explanation: Residential stamp duty is 1% on consideration up to €1 million, so €380,000 x 1% = €3,800. There is no general first-time buyer exemption, and Budget 2027 did not introduce one.
questions.reference: Revenue - residential stamp duty rates (1% / 2% / 6%), as of 2026

questions.question: As of 2026, what stamp duty is payable on the purchase of a residential property for €1,200,000?
questions.explanation: 1% on the first €1,000,000 = €10,000, plus 2% on the next €200,000 = €4,000, giving €14,000 (the 6% rate applies only to the portion above €1.5 million). Applying a single rate to the whole price gives €12,000 or €24,000.
questions.reference: Revenue - residential stamp duty bands, as of 2026

questions.question: A new house is sold for €400,000 plus VAT, so the buyer pays €454,000 including VAT. As of 2026, how much stamp duty is payable?
options: Nil, because VAT has been paid
questions.explanation: Stamp duty on a new residential property is charged on the VAT-exclusive price: €400,000 x 1% = €4,000. Charging it on the VAT-inclusive price (€4,540) is a common mistake.
questions.reference: Revenue - stamp duty on new homes (VAT-exclusive consideration)

questions.question: The Help to Buy incentive is designed to:
options: give all buyers a grant towards stamp duty
provide a low-interest mortgage through local authorities
take an equity share in the home in return for part of the price
help first-time buyers of new or self-built homes fund their deposit through a refund of income tax and DIRT paid in previous years
questions.explanation: Help to Buy refunds income tax and DIRT paid over the previous four years to first-time buyers purchasing or self-building a new home to live in, to help with the deposit. As of 2026 the scheme continues and Budget 2027 increased the maximum relief.

questions.question: Under the First Home Scheme, the State and participating lenders:
options: take an equity stake in a new home to bridge the gap between the buyer's mortgage plus deposit and the price, which the buyer can buy back over time
refund the buyer's income tax paid in previous years
give a tax credit on mortgage interest
provide the full mortgage at a fixed rate
questions.explanation: The First Home Scheme is a shared equity scheme for eligible buyers of new homes. It funds part of the purchase price in return for an equity share, which the buyer can redeem in part or full; charges apply after the initial years.

questions.question: The Local Authority Home Loan is best described as:
options: a grant for home improvements for older people
a Government-backed mortgage provided through local authorities for eligible first-time buyers (and some 'fresh start' applicants) who cannot get enough finance from commercial lenders
a shared equity scheme for buyers of new homes
a refund of stamp duty for first-time buyers
questions.explanation: The Local Authority Home Loan is a State-backed mortgage, available through local authorities, aimed at buyers who cannot obtain sufficient finance elsewhere, subject to income and property price limits.

questions.question: The Mortgage Interest Tax Credit introduced in Budget 2024 was aimed mainly at:
options: first-time buyers saving for a deposit
buy-to-let investors with tracker mortgages
homeowners with a mortgage on their principal private residence whose interest payments had increased compared with 2022
people taking out lifetime mortgages
questions.explanation: The Mortgage Interest Tax Credit gave relief based on the increase in interest paid on a principal private residence mortgage compared with 2022, responding to the rise in interest rates. It is a temporary measure that later Budgets extended on a reduced basis.

questions.question: What is the main reason a borrower switches mortgage to another lender?
options: To obtain a lower interest rate or better terms that save money after allowing for switching costs
To avoid having to insure the property
To reset the Central Credit Register record
To change a principal residence into a buy-to-let
questions.explanation: Switching aims to reduce repayments or total interest. The adviser should weigh the savings against costs such as legal and valuation fees and any breakage cost on a fixed rate.

questions.question: Tom would save €150 a month by switching his variable-rate mortgage. The switch will cost him €1,500 in legal fees and a €300 valuation fee, and he receives no cashback or contribution to costs. Roughly how long will it take for the savings to cover the costs?
options: 10 months
2 months
24 months
12 months
questions.explanation: Total costs = €1,500 + €300 = €1,800. €1,800 / €150 = 12 months. 10 months ignores the valuation fee and 2 months ignores the legal fees.

questions.question: Ruairí wants to top up his mortgage to buy a €25,000 car because the mortgage rate is lower than a car loan rate. What is the main disadvantage?
options: Mortgage top-ups cannot be used for cars
The car is paid for over the remaining mortgage term, so total interest may be much higher, and the debt is secured on his home
His mortgage automatically moves to a fixed rate
He loses his entitlement to the Mortgage Interest Tax Credit permanently
questions.explanation: A lower rate over a much longer term can cost more in total than a shorter car loan, and the borrowing is now secured on the home. Matching the loan term to the life of the car is usually better.

questions.question: Aoibhinn's home is valued at €500,000 and her existing mortgage is €200,000. Her lender will lend up to 80% LTV on a top-up. What is the maximum additional amount she could borrow?
questions.explanation: Maximum total lending = 80% x €500,000 = €400,000. Less the existing €200,000, the maximum top-up is €200,000 (subject to affordability). €400,000 is the total limit, not the extra amount.

questions.question: When assessing a buy-to-let mortgage application, a lender will typically focus on:
options: only the applicant's age
whether the expected rent covers the mortgage repayments by a required margin, together with the applicant's overall financial position
whether the property qualifies for Help to Buy
the applicant's pension contributions only
questions.explanation: Buy-to-let lending is assessed largely on rental cover (rent compared with repayments, often stressed) as well as the borrower's wider income, assets and other debts.

questions.question: In outline, how is rental income from an Irish residential investment property taxed for an individual landlord?
options: It is tax-free under rent-a-room relief
It is taxed only as a capital gain when the property is sold
Net rent, after allowable expenses (including mortgage interest, subject to conditions), is taxed as income at the landlord's marginal rates
It is taxed at a flat 20% with no deductions allowed
questions.explanation: Rental profit is taxed as income (Case V). Allowable deductions include mortgage interest on the property, subject to conditions such as registration with the RTB. Rent-a-room relief applies to letting rooms in your own home, not to investment properties.

questions.question: How are funds typically released on a self-build mortgage?
options: In one lump sum before building starts
Only after the house is complete
In stages as construction progresses, each stage usually certified by an architect or engineer
Monthly, at a fixed amount regardless of progress
questions.explanation: Self-build loans are drawn in stages as work reaches agreed points, with a qualified professional certifying progress, so the lender's advances match the value built. Interest is charged only on amounts drawn.

questions.question: Frank and Úna take a bridging loan to buy their new home before selling their current one. What is the main risk?
options: The new home cannot be insured
Bridging loans cannot be repaid early
Bridging loans are always at a fixed rate for ten years
Their current home takes longer to sell or sells for less than expected, leaving them carrying two loans
questions.explanation: Bridging finance relies on the sale of the existing property. Delays or a lower sale price mean higher interest costs and possibly a shortfall.

questions.question: A lifetime mortgage allows an older homeowner to:
options: borrow against their home, with interest usually rolled up and the loan repaid from the estate when they die or move permanently into long-term care
sell part of their home to the provider while continuing to live there
rent their home to a local authority
receive the Help to Buy refund
questions.explanation: With a lifetime mortgage the homeowner keeps ownership and usually makes no repayments; interest compounds and the loan is repaid when the home is sold. Selling a share of the home is home reversion.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a home reversion scheme and a lifetime mortgage?
options: Home reversion is a loan; a lifetime mortgage is a sale
Only a lifetime mortgage lets the homeowner continue to live in the home

Under home reversion the homeowner sells a share of the home to the provider for a lump sum and keeps the right to live there; under a lifetime mortgage the homeowner keeps full ownership and borrows against the home
Home reversion is available only to first-time buyers
questions.explanation: Home reversion is a part sale of the property; the provider receives its share of the sale proceeds later. A lifetime mortgage is borrowing secured on the home, with rolled-up interest.

questions.question: Maureen, aged 70, takes a lifetime mortgage of €50,000 at a fixed 6% a year, with interest rolled up and compounded annually and no repayments. Approximately how much will be owed after 12 years?
questions.explanation: €50,000 x 1.06^12 = €50,000 x 2.012 = about €100,600; at 6% compound the debt roughly doubles in 12 years. €86,000 is the simple-interest answer (€50,000 + 12 x €3,000).
questions.reference: Lifetime mortgages - compounding of rolled-up interest

questions.question: Which group of costs would a mortgaged buyer of a second-hand home typically expect to pay?
options: Legal fees, the lender's valuation fee, stamp duty and Land Registry registration fees
VAT, Help to Buy fees and rent-a-room charges
The seller's Local Property Tax for the last five years and the auctioneer's fee
Capital gains tax and the seller's legal fees
questions.explanation: Buyers normally pay their own solicitor, the valuation, stamp duty and registration fees with Tailte Éireann (Land Registry). The auctioneer's fee and any CGT are generally the seller's costs.

questions.question: Under section 126 of the Consumer Credit Act 1995, in which situation is a lender NOT required to arrange mortgage protection life cover on a housing loan?
options: The borrower is a first-time buyer
The borrower is over 50 when the loan is approved
The LTV is below 80%
The loan is on a tracker rate
questions.explanation: Section 126 exempts loans to borrowers over 50 at approval, loans where the home is not the principal residence, borrowers an insurer would refuse or accept only at a significantly higher premium, and borrowers who already have adequate life cover.

questions.question: Declan, aged 38, is taking a mortgage to buy an apartment he will let to tenants. He lives elsewhere. Which statement best reflects section 126 of the Consumer Credit Act 1995?
options: Mortgage protection is compulsory because he is under 50
Mortgage protection is compulsory for every housing loan
Section 126 does not require mortgage protection because the property is not his principal residence, although the lender may still require cover under its own policy
Section 126 bans lenders from requiring life cover on buy-to-let loans
questions.explanation: The statutory requirement does not apply where the property is not intended as the principal residence of the borrower or dependants. Lenders can still choose to require cover as a commercial condition.

questions.question: Why does a mortgage lender require buildings insurance on the property?
options: To cover the borrower's repayments if they become ill
To protect the property, which is the lender's security, against risks such as fire, with the lender's interest noted on the policy
To repay the mortgage if the borrower dies
To cover the contents of the home
questions.explanation: If the property were destroyed, the lender's security would be lost. Buildings insurance covers rebuilding, and the lender's interest is noted on the policy. Death cover is provided by mortgage protection, not buildings insurance.

questions.question: Mortgage protection on an annuity mortgage is typically arranged as:
options: level term assurance for the original loan amount
an endowment policy that builds up a cash value
income protection that replaces salary during illness
decreasing term assurance, with the sum assured reducing broadly in line with the outstanding mortgage balance
questions.explanation: Because the balance on an annuity mortgage falls over time, mortgage protection is usually decreasing term cover that pays off the estimated outstanding balance on death, which keeps premiums low.

questions.question: Which is a key feature of an overdraft facility?
options: The bank can generally demand repayment of the full balance at any time
It must be repaid in fixed monthly instalments over five years
Interest is charged on the full limit whether or not it is used
It is always secured on the borrower's home
questions.explanation: Overdrafts are typically repayable on demand, and interest is charged only on the amount actually overdrawn. This makes them suitable for short-term fluctuations rather than long-term borrowing.

questions.question: Mark has an agreed overdraft limit of €1,000 and his account goes €300 beyond that limit. What will his bank typically charge on the excess?
options: No interest at all, because the excess was never agreed
Interest at the bank's credit card rate on the whole overdrawn balance
A statutory penalty equal to 10% of his agreed limit
Surcharge interest on the amount over the limit, on top of the normal overdraft interest
questions.explanation: Going beyond an agreed limit (an unauthorised overdraft) usually attracts surcharge interest on the excess in addition to the ordinary overdraft rate, and may also trigger fees set out in the bank's tariff.
questions.reference: Authorised vs unauthorised overdrafts - surcharge interest

questions.question: The interest-free period on credit card purchases normally applies only if:
options: the card is used only in Ireland
the full statement balance is paid by the payment due date
the minimum repayment is paid by the due date
the purchase is over €100
questions.explanation: Card issuers generally waive interest on purchases only when the full balance is cleared by the due date. Paying only the minimum means interest is charged.

questions.question: Compared with purchases, cash withdrawals (cash advances) on a credit card typically:
options: attract interest from the date of the withdrawal with no interest-free period, often at a higher rate and with a handling fee
benefit from a longer interest-free period than purchases
are interest-free if repaid within 12 months
are treated as a separate personal loan with fixed repayments
questions.explanation: Cash advances usually accrue interest from the day they are taken, often at a higher rate than purchases, and a cash handling fee is commonly charged.

questions.question: As of 2026, how much Government stamp duty applies to a personal credit card account in Ireland?
options: €2.50 per year
€0.12 per transaction
€30 per year per credit card account
€5 per year
questions.explanation: Revenue charges stamp duty of €30 a year on each credit card account, regardless of how much the card is used (Budget 2027 did not change this). The €0.12 per withdrawal and €2.50 / €5 caps relate to ATM and combined debit/ATM cards.
questions.reference: Revenue - stamp duty on financial cards (as of 2026)

questions.question: Aisling pays only the minimum repayment on her credit card each month and makes no new purchases. What is the main consequence?
options: The card provider must convert the balance to an interest-free loan
The balance is cleared within 12 months in any event
Her credit limit automatically increases
The balance is repaid very slowly and she pays much more interest overall
questions.explanation: Minimum repayments are set low, often little more than the interest plus a small amount of capital, so the balance falls slowly and the total interest paid is high.

questions.question: How does a revolving credit facility differ from a personal term loan?
options: It is always secured on property
The borrower can redraw amounts repaid, up to an agreed limit, without making a new application
It carries no interest while the borrower is employed
It has a fixed repayment schedule ending on a set date
questions.explanation: With revolving credit (such as a credit card or revolving account), repaid amounts become available to borrow again up to the limit. A term loan is drawn once and repaid on a fixed schedule.

questions.question: Under a hire-purchase agreement, when does ownership of the goods pass to the hirer?
options: When the agreement is signed
When one-third of the hire-purchase price has been paid
When half of the hire-purchase price has been paid
Only when the final payment, including any option-to-purchase fee, has been made
questions.explanation: Under HP the finance company owns the goods until all payments are made and the option to purchase is exercised. The one-third and one-half thresholds relate to repossession and termination rights, not ownership.

questions.question: Under the Consumer Credit Act 1995, a hirer who ends a hire-purchase agreement early and returns the goods is generally liable to bring the total paid up to:
options: one-third of the hire-purchase price
the full hire-purchase price
one-half of the hire-purchase price
nothing further, as returning the goods ends all liability
questions.explanation: The hirer may terminate at any time and, in general, must pay any amount needed to bring total payments up to half of the hire-purchase price (plus any arrears, and compensation if the goods were not reasonably cared for). Returning the goods alone does not end liability where less than half has been paid.
questions.reference: Consumer Credit Act 1995 - hirer's right to terminate ('half rule')

questions.question: Once a hirer has paid at least one-third of the hire-purchase price, the owner (finance company):
options: cannot repossess the goods without a court order
may repossess the goods immediately after any missed payment without notice
must transfer ownership of the goods to the hirer
loses the right to sue for any arrears
questions.explanation: Under the Consumer Credit Act 1995, once one-third of the HP price has been paid or tendered, the goods are 'protected' and the owner cannot recover them from the hirer except by court action.
questions.reference: Consumer Credit Act 1995 - protected goods ('one-third rule')

questions.question: Paddy has a car on hire purchase with a total HP price of €24,000. He has paid €9,000 and has now fallen into arrears. The finance company proposes to collect the car from his driveway without going to court. Which statement is correct?
options: It may do so, because Paddy is in arrears
It may do so, because the finance company owns the car until the final payment
It may not do so, because more than one-third of the HP price has been paid, so a court order is needed
It may do so, because less than half of the HP price has been paid
questions.explanation: One-third of €24,000 is €8,000. Paddy has paid €9,000, so the car is protected and the finance company must go to court to recover it, even though it still owns the car.

questions.question: Orla's hire-purchase agreement has a total HP price of €20,000. She has paid €6,000, has no arrears and the goods are in good condition. She wants to terminate and return the goods. Under the half rule, what is the maximum further amount she would normally have to pay?
questions.explanation: Half the HP price is €10,000. She has paid €6,000, so she must bring payments up to €10,000 by paying a further €4,000. €10,000 ignores what she has already paid and €14,000 is the full outstanding balance.
questions.reference: Consumer Credit Act 1995 - half rule calculation

questions.question: In a Personal Contract Plan (PCP), the Guaranteed Minimum Future Value (GMFV) is:
options: the deposit the customer must pay at the start
the total of the monthly payments over the agreement
the trade-in value of the customer's old car
the minimum value the finance company guarantees the car will have at the end, which is the optional final payment to keep the car
questions.explanation: The GMFV is set at the start and is the amount the customer pays at the end if they want to own the car. If the car is worth less than the GMFV, the customer can hand it back instead.

questions.question: Which set of choices is normally available to a PCP customer at the end of the agreement?
options: Pay the GMFV and keep the car, return the car (subject to mileage and condition terms), or trade it in and use any equity towards a new agreement
Keep the car with no further payment, since ownership passes once the monthly payments are made
Convert the outstanding GMFV into an interest-free credit card balance
Return the car only if it has done fewer miles than the original owner estimated
questions.explanation: A PCP is a form of hire purchase with a large deferred final payment. At the end the customer can pay it and own the car, hand the car back, or trade in and use any value above the GMFV as a deposit on a new car.
questions.reference: PCP - options at the end of the agreement

questions.question: Why are monthly PCP payments usually lower than hire-purchase payments for the same car, deposit, rate and term?
options: PCP agreements are interest-free
The GMFV is deferred to the end and not repaid through the monthly payments, although interest is charged on it throughout
PCP customers receive a Government subsidy
Under PCP the customer owns the car from the start, so no security is needed
questions.explanation: Under PCP a large part of the price (the GMFV) is left outstanding until the end, so monthly payments repay less capital. Interest is still charged on the whole amount financed, so the total cost of credit can be higher.

questions.question: At the end of a PCP, the market value of Gavin's car is below the GMFV. He has kept within the agreed mileage and the car is in good condition. What can he do?
options: He must pay the difference between the market value and the GMFV
He must keep the car and pay the GMFV
He can hand the car back and the finance company bears the shortfall
He must extend the agreement until the car's value reaches the GMFV
questions.explanation: The guarantee means the finance company carries the risk that the car is worth less than the GMFV, provided the mileage and condition terms are met. Gavin can simply return the car.

questions.question: Under a consumer hire (leasing) agreement, the customer:
options: rents the goods for a period and has no option under the agreement to become the owner
becomes the owner after the final payment
becomes the owner once one-third of the payments are made
must pay a GMFV to return the goods
questions.explanation: A consumer hire agreement is a rental: the goods remain the owner's property and the agreement does not give the hirer an option to buy. That option is what distinguishes hire purchase.
questions.reference: Consumer hire agreements - Consumer Credit Act 1995

questions.question: Why does a credit union often require a borrowing member to keep a certain level of shares while a loan is outstanding?
options: Shares earn a guaranteed dividend that is paid to the lender
Credit unions are prohibited from lending more than the member's shares
Shares are needed to pay the Government stamp duty on the loan
The shares can be held against the loan as security, reducing the credit union's risk
questions.explanation: Credit unions can hold (attach) a member's shares against an outstanding loan, so the shares provide security. A record of regular saving also helps show the member's ability to repay.
questions.reference: Credit union lending - shares as security

questions.question: As of 2026, what is the maximum interest rate an Irish credit union may charge on a loan?
options: 1% per week, calculated as simple interest
1% per month on the reducing balance, inclusive of charges
2.83% per month on the reducing balance
There is no statutory maximum
questions.explanation: The Credit Union Act 1997 caps credit union loan interest at 1% per month on the declining balance (roughly 12.7% APR). The Credit Union (Amendment) Act 2023 allows the Minister for Finance to change the cap by order, but as of 2026 it remains 1% per month. The 1% per week and 2.83% per month figures are high cost credit caps.
questions.reference: Credit Union Act 1997 (as amended 2023) - interest rate cap, as of 2026

questions.question: Loan protection insurance provided by most credit unions typically:
options: repays the member's loan instalments if they become unemployed
clears the outstanding loan balance if the member dies (subject to eligibility), with the premium usually paid by the credit union
is a compulsory policy the member must buy from an outside insurer
repays the loan to the member's guarantor if the member defaults
questions.explanation: Loan protection is a group life cover arranged by the credit union that repays an eligible member's loan on death; the cost is usually borne by the credit union rather than charged separately to the member. It does not cover unemployment.

questions.question: Under the Consumer Credit (Amendment) Act 2022 and the regulations made under it, as of 2026 interest on a high cost credit (moneylending) loan is capped at:
options: 1% per month on the reducing balance
0.2% per day, compounded
1% per week, calculated on a simple interest basis
There is no cap; only APR disclosure is required
questions.explanation: Since November 2022 high cost credit loans are capped at simple interest of 1% per week (with a separate monthly cap for running accounts). 1% per month is the credit union cap.
questions.reference: Consumer Credit (Amendment) Act 2022 - high cost credit interest cap, as of 2026

questions.question: A bridging loan is mainly used to:
options: cover a short gap between buying a new property and receiving the proceeds from selling an existing one
consolidate credit card debts over 20 years
fund a student's living costs while studying
lease a car with no option to buy
questions.explanation: A bridging loan provides short-term finance until an expected sum (usually sale proceeds) is received. Its main risk is that the sale is delayed or achieves less than expected.

questions.question: Emer has three years left on a personal loan and wants a further €5,000. Her lender offers a 'top-up' that adds the €5,000 to her existing balance and sets a new five-year term. What should her adviser point out?
options: The additional €5,000 will be interest-free
Top-ups can only be offered by a different lender
The remaining term will automatically be shortened
The existing balance will now be repaid over a longer period, so she should compare the total cost with a separate new loan for the €5,000
questions.explanation: Topping up and resetting the term spreads the old debt over a longer period, which can increase total interest even if the monthly repayment looks affordable. Comparing total cost with a separate loan is good practice.

questions.question: Which statement about payment protection insurance (PPI) sold with a personal loan is correct?
options: It is optional and the borrower must be told it is not a condition of getting the loan
It is compulsory for all unsecured loans over €5,000
It always covers self-employed borrowers for loss of income
It repays the full loan if the borrower changes job voluntarily
questions.explanation: PPI is an optional product: the consumer must be told it is optional and should only buy it if it is suitable and they are eligible to claim. Many policies restrict cover for the self-employed and do not pay for voluntary job changes.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection Code - payment protection insurance

questions.question: Which borrower is most likely to have an unemployment claim on payment protection insurance declined because of a standard exclusion?
options: Anne, a permanent employee for six years who was made redundant without warning two years after taking out cover
Joe, who took out the cover after he had already been told his job was at risk of redundancy
Mary, a full-time employee who lost her job when her employer closed a year after she took out cover
Pat, a permanent civil servant who has never claimed
questions.explanation: PPI policies typically exclude unemployment the policyholder knew about or expected when taking out cover. Unforeseen redundancy after the initial exclusion period is the type of event the cover is designed for.

questions.question: By signing a guarantee for his daughter's loan, Liam:
options: becomes joint owner of anything bought with the loan
is liable only if the lender first takes his daughter to court and she is declared bankrupt
becomes legally liable to repay the debt if his daughter does not
limits his liability to one month's repayments
questions.explanation: A guarantor promises to meet the borrower's obligations if the borrower fails to do so, and can be pursued for the debt covered by the guarantee.

questions.question: Before Liam signs a guarantee, what is the most important point for his adviser to make?
options: The guarantee will improve Liam's own credit score
Liam can cancel the guarantee at any time without the lender's agreement
A guarantee only applies to secured loans
Liam could be pursued for the guaranteed amount if the borrower defaults, it may affect his own ability to borrow, and he should get independent legal advice
questions.explanation: A guarantee is a real contingent liability. Lenders take it into account when assessing the guarantor's own borrowing, and independent legal advice helps ensure the guarantor understands what they are signing.

questions.question: Clodagh occasionally needs up to €1,500 to cover a few days' shortfall before her monthly salary arrives. Which product is most suitable?
options: A five-year personal term loan of €1,500
An agreed overdraft limit on her current account
A Personal Contract Plan
A mortgage top-up
questions.explanation: A short, recurring cash-flow gap suits an agreed overdraft: interest is charged only on the amount used and for the days it is used. A term loan would charge interest on the full amount for years.

questions.question: Kevin wants to borrow €12,000 to replace his kitchen and would like to repay fixed amounts over five years. Which product best suits him?
options: A credit card cash advance
An overdraft
A personal (home improvement) term loan with fixed repayments
A bridging loan
questions.explanation: A term loan gives a set amount repaid in regular instalments over an agreed period, matching a one-off purchase with a medium-term repayment plan.

questions.question: Lisa is buying a €20,000 car. Option A: a personal loan of €20,000 repaid by 60 monthly payments of €390. Option B: hire purchase with a €2,000 deposit, 60 monthly payments of €360 and a €100 option-to-purchase fee. Which option costs less in total, and by how much?
options: Option B, by €1,800
Option A, by €300
Option B, by €1,700
Both cost the same
questions.explanation: Option A total: 60 x €390 = €23,400. Option B total: €2,000 + (60 x €360 = €21,600) + €100 = €23,700. Option A is €300 cheaper. Comparing only the instalments ignores B's deposit and fee.
questions.reference: Comparing cost of credit - loan vs HP

questions.question: When Lisa buys a car using an unsecured personal loan rather than hire purchase:
options: she owns the car from the outset and the loan is not secured on it
the lender owns the car until the loan is repaid
the one-third rule protects her from repossession
she must pay a GMFV at the end of the loan
questions.explanation: With a personal loan the borrower buys the car outright and owns it; the lender has a debt claim but no ownership. Under HP or PCP the finance company owns the car until the final payment.
questions.reference: Personal loan vs hire purchase - ownership

questions.question: Why is it poor practice to use an overdraft to fund a long-term purchase such as a car?
options: Overdrafts cannot be used for purchases over €1,000
Overdraft interest is not tax deductible for consumers
The overdraft is repayable on demand and usually more expensive, so short-term finance is mismatched with a long-term need
Overdrafts must be cleared every month
questions.explanation: Funding a long-term asset with an on-demand facility exposes the borrower to the bank withdrawing or reducing the limit and typically costs more than a term loan.

questions.question: Which feature is found in hire purchase but not in an unsecured personal loan?
options: The finance company keeps ownership of the goods until the final payment, which acts as its security
Repayments are made monthly
Interest is charged on the amount financed
The agreement must be in writing
questions.explanation: Under HP the goods belong to the finance company until the hirer completes the payments and exercises the option to buy, so the goods themselves secure the debt. Monthly payments, interest and written agreements are common to both.

questions.question: Ronan has a credit card balance of €2,000 on which interest is charged at 1.5% per month. Ignoring compounding within the month, how much interest is charged for one month?
questions.explanation: €2,000 x 1.5% = €30 for the month. €360 would be a year's interest at 18% (12 x 1.5%), and €300 or €3 result from misplacing the decimal.

questions.question: Ms Byrne, who has a steady income and is a member of her local credit union, is thinking of taking a €500 loan from a high cost credit provider. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Proceed, because high cost credit is cheaper than a credit union loan
Proceed, because high cost credit loans are not reported to the Central Credit Register
Ask the credit union first, as its loan is likely to cost far less given its much lower interest cap
Use an unauthorised overdraft instead, as it carries no surcharge
questions.explanation: Credit union loans are capped at 1% per month on the reducing balance, while high cost credit can charge up to 1% per week, so a credit union loan should normally be considered first. High cost credit loans of €500 or more are reported to the Central Credit Register.
questions.reference: Comparing credit union and high cost credit

questions.question: Which is a key reason why lending to consumers is regulated?
options: To guarantee that every loan application is approved
To fix the interest rates that all lenders charge
To protect consumers who typically have less information and expertise than lenders, and to support financial stability
To ensure lenders make a minimum level of profit
questions.explanation: Regulation addresses information imbalance between lender and borrower, protects consumers from unsuitable or unaffordable credit, and supports a stable financial system. It does not guarantee approval or set prices generally.

questions.question: Which body is responsible for authorising and supervising lenders such as retail credit firms and for setting consumer protection rules for regulated lenders in Ireland?
options: The Central Bank of Ireland
The Department of Finance
The Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman
The Insolvency Service of Ireland
questions.explanation: The Central Bank authorises and supervises regulated financial service providers and makes consumer protection rules such as the Consumer Protection Code. The FSPO resolves individual complaints but does not authorise firms.

questions.question: A non-bank firm wants to provide cash loans directly to individuals. It will not take deposits. What type of Central Bank authorisation does it typically need?
options: Mortgage credit intermediary
Credit servicing firm
Investment firm under MiFID II
Retail credit firm
questions.explanation: A firm that provides credit directly to natural persons and is not a bank or other authorised entity is a retail credit firm requiring Central Bank authorisation. Intermediaries arrange credit; credit servicing firms manage loans on behalf of owners.

questions.question: What does a credit servicing firm do?
options: Lends money directly to consumers from its own funds
Manages and administers loans, such as collecting repayments and dealing with arrears, on behalf of the legal owner of the loans
Arranges mortgages for consumers in return for commission
Takes deposits from the public
questions.explanation: Credit servicing firms service loans for the loan owner, for example where a fund has bought a loan book. They must be authorised by the Central Bank, which ensures borrowers keep their regulatory protections.

questions.question: Who is responsible for the regulation of credit unions in Ireland?
options: The CCPC
The Department of Social Protection
The Registrar of Credit Unions, within the Central Bank
The Irish League of Credit Unions
questions.explanation: Credit unions are regulated by the Registrar of Credit Unions, part of the Central Bank. The Irish League of Credit Unions is a representative body, not a regulator.

questions.question: To whom may a credit union lend?
options: Its members
Any member of the public
Only businesses in its common bond area
Only other credit unions
questions.explanation: Credit unions lend only to their members, within lending limits and frameworks set by the Central Bank.
questions.reference: Credit Union Act 1997 - lending to members

questions.question: Which statement about high cost credit providers is correct as of 2026?
options: They are unregulated
They are registered with the CCPC and not supervised by the Central Bank
They may charge collection fees on each home visit
They must hold a Central Bank licence and their cash loans are subject to a statutory cost cap
questions.explanation: High cost credit providers (formerly moneylenders) are licensed by the Central Bank, and since the Consumer Credit (Amendment) Act 2022 the cost of their cash loans is capped and collection charges are prohibited.
questions.reference: High cost credit providers; Consumer Credit (Amendment) Act 2022

questions.question: A car dealer arranges hire-purchase and personal loan finance for its customers with a third-party lender, but does not arrange mortgages. Which body maintains the register on which consumer credit intermediaries of this kind appear?
options: The Central Bank, as mortgage credit intermediaries
The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC)
The Insolvency Service of Ireland
Tailte Éireann
questions.explanation: Credit intermediaries arranging consumer credit (other than mortgages) are authorised and registered by the CCPC under the Consumer Credit Act 1995. Mortgage credit intermediaries are authorised by the Central Bank.

questions.question: Under which regime are mortgage credit intermediaries authorised in Ireland?
options: The Consumer Credit Act 1995 provisions on moneylenders
The Personal Insolvency Act 2012
The European Union (Consumer Mortgage Credit Agreements) Regulations 2016, with authorisation from the Central Bank
The Investment Intermediaries Act 1995 only
questions.explanation: Since the 2016 Regulations, firms arranging or advising on mortgage credit for consumers must be authorised by the Central Bank as mortgage credit intermediaries.
questions.reference: European Union (Consumer Mortgage Credit Agreements) Regulations 2016

questions.question: Which activity is within the scope of the Central Bank's Minimum Competency Code?
options: Advising a consumer on a housing loan
Cleaning the bank's branch premises
Preparing the bank's annual statutory accounts
Maintaining the bank's IT systems
questions.explanation: The Minimum Competency Code applies to staff who advise on or sell retail financial products, including housing loans, consumer credit and associated insurances, and staff who supervise them. The QFA is a recognised qualification.

questions.question: Jamie has just joined a lender and does not yet hold a recognised qualification. Under the Minimum Competency Code, how may he provide advice on housing loans?
options: He may not have any contact with mortgage customers until qualified
He may advise unsupervised, provided he discloses that he is unqualified
He may advise on housing loans but not on associated insurance
He may do so only under the supervision of a competent person while he works to obtain the qualification within the permitted period
questions.explanation: The Code allows new staff to perform specified functions under the supervision of a person who meets the competency standards, for a limited period while they obtain a recognised qualification. Disclosure alone does not satisfy the Code.
questions.reference: Minimum Competency Code - supervision of new staff

questions.question: Which topic forms part of the knowledge required of staff providing mortgage credit under the Mortgage Credit Directive requirements reflected in the Minimum Competency Code?
options: Equity research and stock valuation
The property purchase process, valuation of collateral and creditworthiness assessment
Pension transfer value calculations
Marine and aviation insurance
questions.explanation: Mortgage credit staff must know the relevant products and ancillary services, the legal framework, the property purchase process, collateral valuation, creditworthiness assessment and relevant economics. The other topics relate to unrelated product areas.
questions.reference: Mortgage credit knowledge and competence requirements

questions.question: Before recommending a loan, what must a regulated lender or adviser do under the Central Bank's consumer protection rules?
options: Obtain a guarantee from a family member
Check the consumer's political affiliations
Gather sufficient information about the consumer's needs, objectives and personal and financial circumstances
Ask the consumer to sign a waiver of their complaint rights
questions.explanation: Knowing the consumer is the foundation of the suitability and affordability assessment required by the Consumer Protection Code; the firm must gather and record enough information to assess suitability.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection Code - knowing the consumer

questions.question: After assessing a mortgage applicant's needs and affordability, what does the Consumer Protection Code require the regulated entity to give the consumer?
options: A written statement setting out why the recommended product is considered suitable
A guarantee that the interest rate will not rise
A copy of the lender's internal credit policy
A certificate of title
questions.explanation: The Code requires a written statement of suitability explaining why a recommended product is suitable for the consumer's needs, objectives and circumstances. The certificate of title is a solicitor's document.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection Code - statement of suitability

questions.question: Conor wants a top-up loan that, on the lender's assessment, he cannot afford. He says he understands the risk and insists. What should the lender do?
options: Grant the loan, provided Conor signs a declaration that he insisted
Grant a smaller loan without telling Conor why
Grant the loan at a higher interest rate to reflect the risk
Not offer the credit, as the consumer protection rules require lending to be affordable and suitable based on its assessment
questions.explanation: The lender must assess affordability and must not offer credit it has assessed as unsuitable or unaffordable for the consumer. A consumer's insistence or a signed declaration does not override that obligation.

questions.question: Siobhán wants to consolidate several short-term debts into her 25-year mortgage. What should the lender make clear to her?
options: That consolidation always reduces the total amount repaid
That spreading short-term debt over a longer term may increase the total cost of credit, and the debts become secured on her home
That consolidation removes all her debts from the Central Credit Register
That she will no longer need mortgage protection cover
questions.explanation: Lower monthly repayments from consolidation usually come at the cost of more total interest over a longer term, and unsecured debt becomes secured on the home. Consumers must understand these trade-offs.

questions.question: Under the Consumer Protection Code 2025, what is expected of firms in relation to consumers in vulnerable circumstances?
options: They must refuse to lend to any vulnerable consumer
They must refer all vulnerable consumers to MABS before any discussion
They must identify consumers in vulnerable circumstances and provide additional support and clearer communication to avoid harm
They may charge vulnerable consumers higher rates to reflect risk
questions.explanation: The revised Code strengthened requirements to identify consumers in vulnerable circumstances and to provide extra support and clear communications. Blanket refusal to deal with vulnerable consumers is not the expectation.

questions.question: A borrower remains unhappy after receiving her lender's final response to a complaint about mortgage charges. What can she do?
options: Refer the complaint to the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman
Refer it to the Central Bank, which will decide her individual complaint and award compensation
Nothing, as the lender's final response is binding
Refer it to the Insolvency Service of Ireland
questions.explanation: The firm's final response must tell the consumer they can refer the complaint to the FSPO, which independently adjudicates individual complaints. The Central Bank regulates firms but does not resolve individual complaints.

questions.question: Under the Central Bank's SME Lending Regulations, what must a lender do when it declines a small business's credit application?
options: Refer the business automatically to a high cost credit provider
Charge a fee for processing the application
Report the business to the Central Credit Register as being in default
Give the reasons for the decision in writing and explain the business's right to appeal internally
questions.explanation: The SME Regulations require lenders to give written reasons for declining credit and to have an internal appeals process. A declined application is not a default.

questions.question: Under the Consumer Protection Code 2025, which applied from 24 March 2026, how is the definition of 'consumer' notable for lenders to small businesses?
options: It excludes all incorporated businesses
It includes small businesses with an annual turnover below €5 million
It applies only to individuals aged over 18
It includes all businesses regardless of size
questions.explanation: Law firm summaries of the revised Code note that 'consumer' includes small businesses with turnover of less than €5 million, so those businesses benefit from the Code's protections.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection Code 2025 - definition of consumer (as of 2026)

questions.subtopic: Data protection and the Central Credit Register
questions.question: Why may a lender check the Central Credit Register when Ciarán applies for a €15,000 car loan, without relying on his consent?
options: Because the CCR is a public register open to anyone
Because GDPR does not apply to credit decisions
Because the Credit Reporting Act 2013 requires lenders to check the Register for credit applications of €2,000 or more
Because a lender may use any data it holds for any purpose
questions.explanation: As of 2026, lenders must check the CCR for applications of €2,000 or more, so the check is based on a legal obligation rather than consent. The CCR is not public; access is restricted to lenders and the individual.

questions.subtopic: Data protection and the Central Credit Register
questions.question: Which loans must lenders report to the Central Credit Register?
options: Loans of €500 or more
Loans of €2,000 or more
Only mortgages
Only loans in arrears
questions.explanation: As of 2026, the CCR holds information on loans of €500 or more, whether performing or not. €2,000 is the threshold above which lenders must check the Register.

questions.question: Patricia makes a subject access request to her lender under the GDPR. Within what period must the lender generally respond?
options: Within 10 days
Within six months
Within 40 business days
Within one month, extendable by two further months for complex requests
questions.explanation: Under the GDPR a controller must respond to a subject access request without undue delay and within one month, which may be extended by two further months where necessary, telling the individual of the extension.

questions.question: A lender decides to keep the full personal and financial details of all declined loan applicants indefinitely so it can target them with marketing in future. Which data protection principle is most clearly at risk?
options: Accuracy
Storage limitation and purpose limitation
Data portability
Integrity and confidentiality
questions.explanation: Data collected to assess a loan application should be kept no longer than necessary and not used for an incompatible purpose. Indefinite retention for marketing breaches storage limitation and purpose limitation.

questions.question: Under anti-money laundering law, what must a lender do before entering into a loan relationship with a new borrower?
options: Obtain a guarantee from the borrower's employer
Register the loan with the Land Registry
Carry out customer due diligence, including verifying the borrower's identity
Notify the Gardaí of every new loan
questions.explanation: The Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) Act 2010 requires customer due diligence, including identity verification, before establishing a business relationship. Reports to authorities are needed only where there is suspicion.
questions.reference: Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) Act 2010 - CDD

questions.question: Why does a mortgage lender ask a first-time buyer for evidence of where her €40,000 deposit came from, such as bank statements or a gift letter?
options: To establish the source of funds as part of anti-money laundering checks and to confirm the deposit is genuinely available
To calculate the stamp duty on the purchase
To decide which interest rate to charge
Because the Family Home Protection Act 1976 requires it
questions.explanation: Lenders verify the source of deposit funds to meet AML obligations and to be satisfied the deposit is genuine and not borrowed in a way that affects affordability.

questions.question: Aisling, who works for a lender, notices that a borrower with a modest income has repaid €60,000 of his loan in cash, with no explanation of where the money came from. What should she do?
options: Ask the borrower whether he is laundering money
Refuse the payment and close the account immediately without recording anything
Ignore it, because repaying a loan early cannot be money laundering
Report her suspicion internally to the firm's Money Laundering Reporting Officer under its procedures, without alerting the borrower
questions.explanation: Unexplained lump-sum repayments can be used to launder money. Staff should report suspicions internally to the MLRO, who decides on reporting to FIU Ireland and the Revenue Commissioners; alerting the customer risks tipping off.

questions.question: What is 'tipping off' under anti-money laundering law?
options: Telling a customer the interest rate is about to rise
Disclosing to a customer, or another person, information likely to prejudice an investigation, such as that a suspicious transaction report has been made
Reporting a suspicion to FIU Ireland
Asking a customer for proof of address
questions.explanation: Tipping off is a criminal offence: disclosing that a report has been made or an investigation is under way, in a way likely to prejudice it. Making a report is the required action, not tipping off.
questions.reference: Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) Act 2010 - tipping off

questions.question: Why do the MiFID II rules not apply when a bank advises a consumer on a personal loan?
options: Because MiFID II applies only to firms outside the EU
Because personal loans are covered by the Deposit Guarantee Scheme
Because a loan is not a financial instrument under MiFID II, so lending falls under credit regulation instead
Because MiFID II was repealed in 2026
questions.explanation: MiFID II regulates investment services in financial instruments such as shares, bonds and units in funds. Loans are not financial instruments, so they are governed by consumer credit legislation and the Consumer Protection Code.

questions.question: What is the general time limit for bringing a complaint to the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman?
options: Within 6 years of the conduct complained of (with an alternative period for long-term financial services)
Within 12 months of the conduct
Within 30 days of the provider's final response, with no other limit
There is no time limit
questions.explanation: As of 2026, complaints must generally be made within 6 years of the conduct; for long-term financial services there is an alternative based on 3 years from when the complainant became aware, and the FSPO has some discretion to extend.

questions.question: As of 2026, what is the maximum compensation the FSPO can direct a financial service provider to pay on a complaint about a loan?
questions.explanation: The FSPO can direct compensation of up to €500,000 (as of 2026); the lower €52,000 limit applies to annuity complaints. It can also direct the provider to rectify the conduct.

questions.question: What must a borrower normally do before the FSPO will investigate his complaint about a lender?
options: Pay a fee to the FSPO
Complain to the lender first and give it the opportunity to resolve the complaint
Obtain a court judgment
Get the Central Bank's permission
questions.explanation: The FSPO's service is free, but the consumer must first complain to the provider and allow it to deal with the complaint through its own process before the FSPO will investigate.

questions.question: A borrower asks whether the Deposit Guarantee Scheme protects her if her mortgage lender fails. What is the correct answer?
options: Yes, the scheme repays up to €100,000 of her mortgage
Yes, the scheme cancels her mortgage
No, the scheme protects eligible deposits, not loans; her mortgage remains owed
No, because the scheme only covers business accounts
questions.explanation: The Deposit Guarantee Scheme protects eligible deposits up to €100,000 per depositor per institution; it does not cover loans, which remain owed to the lender or whoever acquires the loan.

questions.question: What does the Central Bank's fitness and probity regime require of people in controlled functions at a regulated lender?
options: That they are competent and capable, honest, ethical and act with integrity, and are financially sound
That they hold shares in the lender
That they have worked in banking for at least 20 years
That they are Irish citizens
questions.explanation: The fitness and probity standards require people in controlled functions to be fit (competent and capable) and proper (honest, ethical, acting with integrity and financially sound). Pre-approval controlled functions need Central Bank approval before appointment.

questions.question: Which is a component of the Central Bank's Individual Accountability Framework introduced under the Central Bank (Individual Accountability Framework) Act 2023?
options: A cap on bankers' bonuses at 100% of salary
A requirement for all bank staff to hold the QFA
A ban on lending to company directors
Conduct Standards that apply to individuals performing controlled functions, such as acting with honesty and integrity
questions.explanation: The IAF includes the Senior Executive Accountability Regime, Conduct Standards for individuals in controlled functions, enhancements to fitness and probity, and changes to the administrative sanctions procedure.

questions.question: What distinguishes a credit institution, such as a bank, from a retail credit firm?
options: A credit institution may lend only to businesses
A credit institution takes deposits from the public as well as granting credit
A credit institution is regulated by the CCPC
A credit institution cannot provide mortgages
questions.explanation: A credit institution's defining feature is taking deposits or other repayable funds from the public and granting credit. Retail credit firms lend to individuals but do not take deposits.
questions.reference: Credit institutions vs retail credit firms

questions.question: What is the main reason a lender takes security for a loan?
options: To remove the need to assess the borrower's ability to repay from income
To provide a secondary source of repayment if the borrower fails to repay from income
To transfer ownership of the asset to the lender for the term of the loan
To allow the lender to charge a higher interest rate than on an unsecured loan
questions.explanation: Security is a fallback: the primary source of repayment is always the borrower's income or cash flow, and security is realised only if that fails. Taking security never replaces the repayment capacity assessment.
questions.reference: Principles of lending - role of security

questions.question: Judged on stability of value, certainty of title and ease of realisation, which of the following is generally the strongest security for a lender?
options: Specialised machinery used only in the borrower's own business
Shares in a small private company owned by the borrower's family
A cash deposit held with the lending bank itself, subject to a charge or right of set-off
A five-year-old car registered in the borrower's name
questions.explanation: A deposit held by the lender has a known, stable value, clear title and can be applied against the debt without a sale. Machinery, private company shares and cars are harder to value, can depreciate quickly and must be sold to realise value.
questions.reference: Attributes of good security - value, title, realisation

questions.question: Why are shares in an unquoted private company usually regarded as weak security?
options: Because a lender is legally prohibited from taking a charge over company shares
Because their value is guaranteed by the company and so adds nothing
Because they automatically transfer to the lender if the company makes a loss
Because they are difficult to value and to sell, and transfers are often restricted by the company's constitution
questions.explanation: Good security should be easy to value and realise. Unquoted shares have no ready market, their value depends on the company's fortunes and the constitution often restricts who they can be transferred to.
questions.reference: Attributes of good security - ease of realisation

questions.question: A property is sold by the lender for €300,000 after the borrower defaults. The first legal charge secures €250,000 and a second charge secures €80,000. Ignoring costs, how much does the second chargeholder receive from the proceeds?
options: Nothing, because a second charge is unenforceable
questions.explanation: The first chargeholder is paid in full first (€250,000), leaving €300,000 - €250,000 = €50,000 for the second chargeholder. The remaining €30,000 owed to the second chargeholder becomes an unsecured residual debt.

questions.question: For registered land in Ireland, how is the priority between two registered charges over the same property generally determined?
options: By the size of each loan, with the larger loan ranking first
By the date each loan offer was issued
By the order in which the charges are registered on the folio
By agreement of the borrower at the time of default
questions.explanation: For registered land, priority between registered charges generally follows the order of registration in the Land Registry, which is why lenders insist on prompt registration (subject to any priority agreement between the chargeholders).
questions.reference: Land Registry - priority of registered charges

questions.question: Which body now operates the Land Registry and the Registry of Deeds in Ireland?
options: The Central Bank of Ireland
The Courts Service
The Revenue Commissioners
Tailte Éireann
questions.explanation: Tailte Éireann was established in 2023, bringing together the Property Registration Authority (Land Registry and Registry of Deeds), Ordnance Survey Ireland and the Valuation Office.

questions.question: In registered title, what is a folio?
options: The solicitor's file of title deeds for unregistered land
The register entry for a property recording its description, the registered owner and burdens such as charges
The valuer's report confirming the property's market value
A memorial lodged in the Registry of Deeds to protect priority
questions.explanation: Each registered property has a folio in the Land Registry (with a linked map) showing the property, the owner and burdens such as registered charges. Title deeds and memorials relate to unregistered land.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the Registry of Deeds?
options: It records deeds affecting unregistered land, mainly to establish priority between them, but does not guarantee title
It guarantees the title of the registered owner shown on the folio
It is the register of charges created by companies
It records only leases of more than 21 years
questions.explanation: Unregistered title is proved by the chain of title deeds; registering a deed in the Registry of Deeds protects its priority but does not guarantee title. The State-backed guarantee of title applies to registered land in the Land Registry.
questions.reference: Registry of Deeds vs Land Registry

questions.question: Niamh wants a mortgage on a leasehold apartment. Which feature of the title will the lender be most concerned about?
options: Whether the apartment was built before or after 1976
Whether Niamh holds the title jointly with a sibling
The unexpired term of the lease and the obligations in the lease such as service charges
Whether the freehold is registered in the Registry of Deeds rather than the Land Registry
questions.explanation: A leasehold interest lasts only for the term of the lease, so the lender needs enough unexpired term to cover the loan and leave the property saleable, and must consider lease covenants such as service charges that affect value and saleability.

questions.question: In Irish residential lending, the lender usually releases the loan funds before its mortgage is registered. What mainly protects the lender during this gap?
options: The Deposit Guarantee Scheme
A guarantee from the estate agent
The borrower's mortgage protection policy
The borrower's solicitor's undertaking to the lender to secure good marketable title and register the lender's charge
questions.explanation: The borrower's solicitor gives a professional undertaking to obtain good marketable title, have the lender's charge registered and hold the title documents for the lender. Breach of an undertaking is serious professional misconduct, which gives the lender comfort.

questions.question: In the Irish residential mortgage process, what is the purpose of the certificate of title given by the borrower's solicitor?
options: It certifies the market value of the property for loan-to-value purposes
It confirms to the lender that the borrower has good marketable title and that the lender's mortgage is or will be a first legal charge
It records the consent of the borrower's spouse under the Family Home Protection Act 1976
It confirms that stamp duty has been refunded
questions.explanation: Under the certificate of title system the lender relies on the borrower's solicitor to investigate title and certify that it is good and marketable and that the lender will hold a first legal charge. Value is confirmed separately by the valuation.

questions.question: Declan owns the family home in his sole name and is married to Sinéad. He wants to mortgage the home. What does the Family Home Protection Act 1976 require?
options: Sinéad's prior consent in writing to the mortgage
Sinéad's consent only if she contributed to the purchase price
Notice to Sinéad within 30 days after the mortgage is signed
Court approval, because the home is in one name only
questions.explanation: A conveyance of an interest in the family home, which includes a mortgage, by the owning spouse requires the prior written consent of the non-owning spouse, regardless of whether that spouse contributed financially.

questions.question: What is the effect, in general, of a mortgage of a family home granted without the required prior written consent of the non-owning spouse?
options: It is valid but the lender must pay compensation to the spouse
It is valid once the spouse is informed after completion
It is void, subject to the limited protections in the Act for certain purchasers
It converts automatically into an unsecured loan
questions.explanation: The 1976 Act provides that a conveyance (including a mortgage) of the family home made without the prior written consent of the other spouse is void, subject to limited exceptions. This is why lenders insist on the consent and on evidence of marital status.

questions.question: Which legislation gives a civil partner protection equivalent to the Family Home Protection Act 1976 where the other civil partner proposes to mortgage their shared home?
options: The Consumer Credit Act 1995
The Land and Conveyancing Law Reform Act 2009
The Family Law Act 1995
The Civil Partnership and Certain Rights and Obligations of Cohabitants Act 2010
