questions.explanation: The 2010 Act requires the prior written consent of the non-owning civil partner to a conveyance, including a mortgage, of the shared home, mirroring the 1976 Act protection for spouses.
questions.reference: Civil Partnership and Certain Rights and Obligations of Cohabitants Act 2010

questions.question: Ronan executed a mortgage over the family home, which is in his sole name, on 3 March. His wife Maeve signed a consent form on 4 March. What is the lender's position?
options: The mortgage is fully protected because Maeve consented within a reasonable time
The mortgage is at risk because the consent was not given before the mortgage was executed
The mortgage is protected because Maeve is not a borrower
The consent is valid because it was in writing, and timing does not matter
questions.explanation: The Act requires the non-owning spouse's consent to be given in writing before the conveyance. A consent signed after the mortgage was executed does not satisfy the Act, leaving the mortgage open to challenge as void.
questions.reference: Family Home Protection Act 1976 - prior written consent

questions.subtopic: Joint tenancy and tenancy in common
questions.question: Seán and Úna own their home as joint tenants. Seán dies, and his will leaves everything to his brother. Who owns the home?
options: Úna, by the right of survivorship
Seán's brother and Úna in equal shares
Seán's brother, under the will
Seán's estate, until the mortgage is repaid
questions.explanation: Under a joint tenancy the right of survivorship means the deceased's interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant, outside the will. A will can only pass a share held as a tenant in common.

questions.subtopic: Joint tenancy and tenancy in common
questions.question: Which feature is characteristic of a tenancy in common?
options: Each co-owner's interest passes automatically to the other co-owners on death
Co-owners must always hold equal shares
Each co-owner holds a distinct share that passes under their will or intestacy on death
Only married couples may hold property this way
questions.explanation: Tenants in common hold separate (possibly unequal) shares with no right of survivorship, so each share forms part of the owner's estate on death. Automatic passing to survivors is the feature of a joint tenancy.

questions.question: What is the nature of a guarantor's liability under a guarantee?
options: The guarantor becomes the owner of the asset bought with the loan
The guarantor is liable only for interest, not for capital
The guarantor is jointly responsible for making every monthly repayment from the start
The guarantor is liable to pay if the principal borrower fails to pay
questions.explanation: A guarantee is a secondary obligation: the guarantor promises to pay the debt if the principal debtor defaults. The guarantor is not a borrower and does not own the asset.

questions.question: Eoin's mother has agreed to guarantee his business loan. Why will the lender usually insist that she obtains independent legal advice before signing?
options: Because a guarantee is not legally binding without a solicitor's signature
To reduce the risk that the guarantee is later set aside on grounds such as undue influence or misunderstanding
Because the Consumer Credit Act 1995 requires every guarantor to be legally represented
So that the solicitor becomes jointly liable with the guarantor
questions.explanation: Where a guarantor has a close relationship with the borrower and gains no direct benefit, a court may set the guarantee aside for undue influence or misrepresentation. Independent advice that the guarantor understood the commitment strengthens the lender's position.

questions.question: Ciara and Mark took out a joint loan of €20,000 with joint and several liability. Mark has emigrated and stopped paying. What can the lender do?
options: Pursue Ciara for the full outstanding balance
Pursue Ciara for only half of the outstanding balance
Pursue only Mark, as he caused the default
Nothing until both borrowers can be located
questions.explanation: Joint and several liability means each borrower is liable for the whole debt as well as jointly with the other, so the lender can recover the full balance from Ciara. Any claim she has against Mark is a matter between them.

questions.question: Which event is most likely to release a guarantor from liability, if the guarantee contains no clause dealing with it?
options: The principal borrower makes one late payment
The lender sends the guarantor an annual statement
The lender and borrower agree a material variation of the loan terms without the guarantor's consent
The guarantor moves to a new address
questions.explanation: At common law a material variation of the principal contract made without the guarantor's consent can discharge the guarantor, because the risk guaranteed has changed. Lenders therefore draft guarantees to permit variations or obtain the guarantor's consent.

questions.question: A lender takes an assignment of a borrower's life policy as security. What step should the lender take to protect its position?
options: Register the assignment on the property folio
Ask the borrower to stop paying the premiums
Have the policy surrendered immediately
Give written notice of the assignment to the life assurance company
questions.explanation: Notice to the insurer ensures the insurer pays the policy proceeds to the lender as assignee and protects the lender's priority. Premiums must continue to be paid for the policy to remain in force.

questions.question: Which type of life policy offers a lender security value during the borrower's lifetime, not just on death?
options: A level term assurance policy
A policy with a cash or surrender value, such as a with-profits whole-of-life or endowment policy
A mortgage protection (decreasing term) policy
A serious illness policy with no investment element
questions.explanation: Only a policy with an accumulated cash or surrender value can be realised while the life assured is alive. Term and mortgage protection policies pay out only on a claim and have no surrender value.

questions.question: Gráinne's credit union loan is secured partly by her shares in the credit union, which are attached to the loan. What does this mean for Gráinne?
options: She generally cannot withdraw the attached shares while the loan they secure is outstanding
Her shares are cancelled and replaced by the loan
She can withdraw the shares at any time, as security over credit union shares is not permitted
The credit union must pay her a higher dividend on attached shares
questions.explanation: Shares attached or pledged to a loan act like a lien over a deposit: the credit union can refuse withdrawal and, if necessary, set them off against the debt. This gives the lender easily realisable security.
questions.reference: Lien over deposits and credit union shares

questions.question: Which statement best describes a chattel mortgage?
options: A charge over land registered on the folio
An assignment of a life policy to a lender
Security over movable goods, such as machinery or vehicles, that usually remain in the borrower's possession
A guarantee given by a company director
questions.explanation: A chattel mortgage gives the lender security over personal movable property while the borrower keeps using it. Because the goods are portable and depreciate, it is generally weaker security and must be properly registered.

questions.question: Why will a lender normally decline to lend to a 17-year-old in his own name without further arrangements?
options: Because a minor cannot open a bank account
Because the Consumer Credit Act 1995 sets a minimum loan size for young people
Because a minor cannot be the subject of a Central Credit Register report
Because a loan contract with a minor is generally not enforceable against the minor
questions.explanation: A person under 18 generally lacks full contractual capacity and a loan agreement is generally unenforceable against them, so the lender could not rely on the contract. A lender may consider other arrangements, such as an adult borrower.

questions.question: A company grants a lender a charge over its premises. What must be done for the charge to be effective against a liquidator and the company's other creditors?
options: The directors must give personal guarantees
Particulars of the charge must be registered with the Companies Registration Office within 21 days of its creation
The charge must be approved by the Central Bank
The shareholders must each sign the loan agreement
questions.explanation: Under the Companies Act 2014 a charge created by a company must be registered with the CRO within 21 days, otherwise it is void against a liquidator and creditors. Lenders also check the company's capacity and board authority to borrow.

questions.question: Why does a mortgage lender require a valuation of the property by a valuer on its panel?
options: To confirm the property's market value supports the loan and that the property is acceptable security
To confirm the borrower has good marketable title
To calculate the stamp duty payable
To replace the need for a structural survey by the buyer
questions.explanation: The valuation tells the lender whether the property's market value supports the loan-to-value and whether it is readily saleable security. Title is the solicitor's role, and a lender's valuation is not a substitute for the buyer's own survey.

questions.question: A property is valued at €400,000 and the requested mortgage is €320,000. What is the loan-to-value ratio?
questions.explanation: LTV = loan / value = €320,000 / €400,000 = 80%. 125% is value divided by loan (inverted) and 20% is the deposit as a share of value.

questions.question: In outline, how does a lender usually enforce its mortgage over a borrower's family home in Ireland where arrears cannot be resolved?
options: It registers a judgment mortgage and waits for the borrower to sell
It changes the locks once three payments are missed
It takes ownership of the home and keeps any surplus on sale
It applies to court for an order for possession and then sells the property, applying the proceeds to the debt
questions.explanation: A lender seeking possession of a principal residence must go through the courts; once it obtains possession it can sell under its power of sale. Any surplus after the debt and costs belongs to the borrower, and any shortfall remains owed.

questions.question: A lender holds a mortgage over a borrower's buy-to-let property that is in arrears. Which remedy is commonly used to collect the rent and manage or sell the property?
options: Applying for a Debt Relief Notice
Appointing a receiver under the mortgage
Petitioning for the borrower's bankruptcy as a first step
Registering a lien on the borrower's deposit account
questions.explanation: Mortgages over investment property usually give the lender power to appoint a receiver, who can collect rents and manage or sell the property, typically acting as agent of the borrower.

questions.question: What does a creditor achieve by registering a judgment mortgage?
options: It cancels the debtor's existing first legal charge
It obtains a court order for possession of the family home
It turns a court judgment for an unsecured debt into a charge on the debtor's land
It prevents the debtor from entering a Personal Insolvency Arrangement
questions.explanation: A creditor with a court judgment can register a judgment mortgage against the debtor's interest in land, giving it secured status ranking behind existing charges. It does not by itself give possession.

questions.question: What is negative equity?
options: Where the outstanding mortgage balance is greater than the market value of the property
Where monthly repayments exceed 35% of net income
Where a borrower has missed three or more repayments
Where a property's value has fallen by more than 10% in a year
questions.explanation: Negative equity arises when the debt secured on a property exceeds its value, so a sale would not clear the loan. It is not itself a measure of arrears or affordability.

questions.question: Paul owes €280,000 on his mortgage. The property is sold for €230,000 and the sale costs €10,000. Assuming no other payments, what is his residual debt?
options: Nil, because the security has been realised
questions.explanation: Net proceeds are €230,000 - €10,000 = €220,000, so the residual debt is €280,000 - €220,000 = €60,000. €50,000 ignores the sale costs; realising the security does not extinguish the shortfall.

questions.question: After a voluntary sale, a shortfall remains on Aisling's mortgage. Which statement is correct?
options: The shortfall is automatically written off because the borrower co-operated
The shortfall remains owed as an unsecured debt, although the lender may agree a repayment arrangement or settlement
The shortfall transfers to the buyer of the property
The shortfall can only be recovered if Aisling buys another property
questions.explanation: Selling the security does not extinguish the loan; any residual debt continues as an unsecured liability. Lenders may agree affordable repayments or a settlement, and insolvency options may also be relevant.
